articles.title: Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer
articles.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation.
articles.content:
For nearly two decades, scientists have known that a common gut bacterium can produce a toxin that damages the colon and helps drive the formation of tumors. What they could not explain was how the toxin first attaches to intestinal cells and begins its attack. Now, researchers have uncovered that missing step, revealing a surprising vulnerability that could lead to new ways of protecting the colon.

The breakthrough comes from a team led by scientists at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, its Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Their findings, published in Nature, identify a protein called claudin-4 as the essential docking point for a bacterial toxin known as BFT.

Even more promising, the researchers have already used this discovery to develop a molecular decoy that intercepts the toxin before it can damage colon cells. The strategy successfully protected mice from the toxin's harmful effects, suggesting a possible new approach to preventing bacterial damage associated with colorectal cancer. The research received partial support from the National Institutes of Health.

"We've made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment," says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. "Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections."

How a Common Gut Bacterium Can Promote Colon Cancer

The investigation centers on Bacteroides fragilis, a bacterium that can be found in the intestines of up to 20% of healthy people. Although the presence of this bacterium does not automatically mean someone will develop cancer, certain strains produce a powerful toxin capable of disrupting the colon's protective lining, causing inflammation, and encouraging tumor growth.

The toxin, known as B. fragilis toxin or BFT, has been under investigation for years. In a landmark 2009 study published in Nature Medicine, Sears and her colleagues demonstrated that the toxin could promote the development of colon tumors. Their work helped establish an important connection between toxin-producing gut bacteria, chronic inflammation, and colorectal cancer.

Earlier experiments also revealed that BFT damages a protein called E-cadherin, which helps hold neighboring cells together and maintain the colon's protective barrier. When this protein is broken apart, the barrier becomes compromised, potentially allowing harmful substances and bacteria to interfere with the surrounding tissue.

However, one critical question remained unanswered. Although BFT could break down E-cadherin, the toxin did not appear to attach directly to that protein. Researchers suspected that another molecule was helping the toxin reach its target, but repeated attempts to identify it had failed.

Scientists Identify the Missing Link Using CRISPR

To solve the mystery, the researchers turned to CRISPR, a powerful gene-editing technology that allows scientists to selectively disable genes and investigate what they do.

Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate working in Sears' laboratory, led a genome-wide CRISPR screening effort in collaboration with Matthew Waldor's laboratory at Harvard Medical School. The team systematically switched off genes in colon epithelial cells, the cells that form the inner lining of the colon, to determine which ones were necessary for the toxin to attach and cause damage.

One gene stood out dramatically. It produces claudin-4, a protein that helps neighboring cells form tight junctions, the seals that limit the movement of substances between cells and help maintain the intestinal barrier.

When the researchers disabled the gene responsible for claudin-4, BFT could no longer bind to the colon cells. Without that initial attachment, the toxin was unable to attack E-cadherin.

The finding revealed that claudin-4 acts as a receptor for the bacterial toxin. In effect, the toxin must first latch onto this protein before it can carry out its damaging activity.

"It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit," says White. "That was an exciting moment."

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a New Bacterial Attack Strategy

The identity of the receptor surprised the scientists.

Sears and other researchers had expected BFT to interact with a protein involved in cellular signaling, such as a G protein-coupled receptor. These receptors act somewhat like communication switches, allowing cells to respond to signals from their surroundings.

Claudin-4, however, serves a very different purpose. Rather than functioning primarily as a signaling receptor, it helps maintain the physical connections between neighboring cells.

The discovery also revealed an unusual way for a bacterial toxin to operate. BFT belongs to a class of enzymes called proteases, which cut other proteins. Most proteases act directly on their targets, but BFT appears to require a separate receptor before it can reach and damage E-cadherin.

When the team reviewed previous scientific research, they could not identify another toxin known to use the same mechanism.

To establish that BFT and claudin-4 truly bind to each other, the Johns Hopkins researchers collaborated with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona.

Using techniques that measure how molecules interact, White and the Barcelona team showed that BFT and claudin-4 form a tightly bound complex in laboratory experiments. Each toxin molecule paired with one receptor molecule, providing direct physical evidence of the connection.

A Clever Molecular Decoy Blocks the Dangerous Gut Toxin

Identifying the receptor did more than explain how the toxin works. It also gave the scientists an idea for stopping it.

If BFT needs claudin-4 to attach to colon cells, perhaps a substitute could lure the toxin away from its intended target.

To test that possibility, the team developed a molecular decoy. This was a soluble protein carrying sequences from claudin-4, designed to attract BFT without allowing it to attack the colon's protective lining.

The researchers then worked with Min Dong's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, including Kang Wang and colleagues, to investigate the approach in mice. These experiments allowed the scientists to examine how the toxin behaves in the more complicated environment of a living intestine.

The results were encouraging. Instead of binding to claudin-4 receptors on colon cells, BFT attached to the decoy proteins. By intercepting the toxin, the decoys successfully protected the mice from BFT-induced damage.

The finding suggests that it may be possible to interfere with the toxin's first step rather than trying to repair the damage after it occurs.

"This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties," says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

Small molecules are compounds that can sometimes be developed into medicines, while biologics are treatments made from or involving biological materials, such as proteins. Future versions of the decoy strategy could potentially be designed to work more effectively in the body or be easier to administer.

What This Discovery Could Mean for Colon Cancer Prevention

Although the findings identify a promising new target, important questions remain.

Scientists have established that BFT attaches to claudin-4 and that blocking this interaction can protect mice from toxin-induced damage. However, they have not yet captured the exact experimental three-dimensional structure showing how the two molecules fit together.

Even advanced artificial intelligence tools, including AlphaFold, have been unable to fully resolve the interaction. Understanding its precise structure could help researchers design more effective compounds that prevent the toxin from binding.

Further experiments will also be needed to determine whether the decoy approach can safely and effectively prevent toxin-related disease in humans. The mouse experiments demonstrated protection against tissue damage, but they did not establish that the strategy prevents colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, the discovery resolves a major question that has persisted since the connection between BFT and colon tumor formation was established in 2009. By identifying the toxin's previously unknown point of attachment, researchers have uncovered a potential way to interrupt a harmful biological process before it begins.

The findings could ultimately support new strategies for detecting or treating conditions associated with bacterial toxins, including colorectal cancer, diarrhea, and bloodstream infections.

Study Authors, Funding, and Disclosures

Additional researchers who contributed to the study include Jason Chen, Shaoguang Wu, Abby L. Geis, and Jessica Queen of Johns Hopkins, along with Hailong Zhang, Karthik Hullahalli, and Jie Zhang of Harvard Medical School.

Funding was provided by the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Janssen Research and Development, Cancer Research UK, the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01 AI042347, R01 NS080833, R01 NS117626, R01 AI170835 and R01 AI189789) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden mechanism that allows high-cholesterol diets to undermine the body's natural cholesterol defenses, and blocking it dramatically lowered harmful LDL cholesterol in mice. Even more promising, an experimental drug targeting this pathway has already passed an early human safety trial, potentially speeding the development of a new treatment for high cholesterol.
articles.content:
Heart disease linked to high cholesterol continues to be the leading cause of death worldwide. Although doctors have more treatment options than ever, many people still struggle to lower their cholesterol to safe levels. Others experience side effects that make existing medications difficult to take.

Researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have now identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why diets high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the body's ability to remove harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the bloodstream. Even more promising, they have identified an experimental drug that has already undergone safety testing in humans and could potentially interfere with this process.

The findings, published in Nature, could open the door to a new approach to treating high cholesterol.

"We've known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver's ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn't fully understand why," said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. "This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle."

How the Liver Removes Bad Cholesterol

The liver plays a central role in controlling cholesterol levels. It removes cholesterol from the bloodstream so it can be processed, broken down, and used by other parts of the body.

To accomplish this, liver cells rely on structures called LDL receptors. Located on the surface of these cells, the receptors work much like docking stations, capturing LDL cholesterol circulating in the blood and bringing it inside for processing.

The number of available receptors matters. When liver cells have more LDL receptors, they can remove more cholesterol from circulation. This is one reason widely used cholesterol medications, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, are effective. They help maintain or increase the number of receptors available to clear LDL cholesterol.

Scientists Uncover a Hidden Cholesterol Pathway

Using experiments involving mice and human cells, the researchers discovered a previously unrecognized process that interferes with the liver's ability to clear cholesterol. Over time, this mechanism reduces the number of LDL receptors, making it harder for the body to keep blood cholesterol under control.

The process begins with a protein known as Ral, which Saltiel had previously investigated in fat cells. The team discovered that consuming high amounts of dietary cholesterol activates Ral, setting off a chain of events that leads to the loss of LDL receptors. As Ral activity increases, fewer receptors remain available to remove harmful cholesterol from the bloodstream.

The researchers then identified another critical piece of the mechanism: an enzyme called cathepsin A (CTSA). This enzyme helps drive the process responsible for depleting LDL receptors.

When scientists used a small molecule inhibitor to block CTSA, the results were striking. LDL receptors became more stable, and levels of circulating LDL cholesterol dropped dramatically in mice.

The discovery is especially significant because the newly identified pathway is different from those targeted by current cholesterol medications. That distinction could make it possible to develop treatments for patients who do not respond adequately to existing drugs.

"There's still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can't get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now," said Saltiel. "This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap."

A Previously Tested Drug Could Accelerate Treatment

Discovering a new biological target is usually only the beginning of a lengthy drug development process. Researchers often need years of additional work to identify a suitable compound and determine whether it can be used safely in people.

In this case, however, the scientists may already have a promising candidate.

A drug designed to inhibit CTSA had previously been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. Although the program was eventually discontinued for strategic reasons, the experimental medication had already progressed through a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully evaluated for safety in humans.

That earlier work could provide an important advantage. Rather than beginning drug development from scratch, researchers believe the existing CTSA inhibitor may be ready to advance into a Phase 2 clinical trial to investigate its effectiveness against high cholesterol.

The findings are still at an early stage, and the drug has not yet been shown to lower cholesterol in humans. Nevertheless, its previous clinical testing could shorten the path toward determining whether this new treatment strategy works in patients.

"Luckily, there's an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that's already been shown to be safe in humans," said Saltiel. "We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial -- which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected."

Co-authors of the study include Xue Feng, Shuo Zhang, Yuqi Wang, Twisha Kurlagunda, Allyssa Sit, Sadatsugu Sakane, Se Yong Park, Churaibhon Wisessaowapak, Kaylee Nguyen, Jamie Yan, Himani Pothulu, Catherine Dinh, Felicia Chu, Yuyao Ren, Bichen Zhang, Patrick Secrest, Chao-Wei Hung, Preethi Veeragandham, Yuliya Skorobogatko, Tatiana Kisseleva, and Amit R. Majithia at UC San Diego; Priya Jaishankar, Pusu Yang, and Adam Renslo at the University of California, San Francisco; Linmeng Han and Peng Zhao at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; and Philip L.S.M. Gordts at the University of Utah.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health (Grants P30DK063491, R01DK117551, R01DK128796, and R01DK135289) and an American Diabetes Association postdoctoral fellowship (1-25-PDF-76).

articles.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
articles.summary: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.
articles.content:
A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.

The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.

The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?

Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance

To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.

At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.

The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.

Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.

Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.

A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans

One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.

The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).

This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.

"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."

Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.

Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.

One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.

"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."

There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.

In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.

Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?

The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.

Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.

Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.

For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.

"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."

articles.personality_title: Simple blood test predicts Alzheimer’s risk years before symptoms
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Alzheimer’s disease causes memory and thinking problems that get worse over time. Detecting who will develop these problems early has been difficult, limiting chances for early care or treatment.

**What happened** – An international team of scientists studied 2,684 older adults without memory problems from North America, Japan, and Australia. They tested their blood for a marker called phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), linked to Alzheimer’s. Those with very high p-tau217 levels had a 38% chance of developing cognitive problems within five years and a 78% chance within 10 years. The study combined data from six long-term research projects dating back to 2004.

**Impact** – This blood test can predict Alzheimer’s risk better than some brain scans and genetic tests. It gives doctors a simple way to find people likely to develop memory issues years before symptoms start. This could help select who might join prevention studies or get early treatment once new medicines are ready.

**What’s next step** – Researchers want to confirm these findings in larger, more diverse groups and over longer times. They are also testing new treatments that could slow or stop Alzheimer’s before symptoms appear. If successful, this blood test might become a routine tool to guide early care, similar to how cholesterol tests help prevent heart disease.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A simple blood test measuring p-tau217 can identify people at higher risk of Alzheimer’s years before symptoms, opening the door to earlier prevention and treatment.

articles.personality_title_es: Un simple análisis de sangre predice el riesgo de Alzheimer años antes de los síntomas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La enfermedad de Alzheimer causa problemas de memoria y pensamiento que empeoran con el tiempo. Saber quién desarrollará estos problemas temprano ha sido difícil, limitando las oportunidades de cuidado o tratamiento precoz.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo internacional estudió a 2,684 adultos mayores sin problemas de memoria en Norteamérica, Japón y Australia. Analizaron su sangre para un marcador llamado tau fosforilada 217 (p-tau217), relacionado con Alzheimer. Quienes tenían niveles muy altos tenían un 38% de riesgo de problemas cognitivos en 5 años y un 78% en 10 años. El estudio combinó datos de seis proyectos de investigación a largo plazo desde 2004.

**Impacto** – Este análisis de sangre puede predecir el riesgo de Alzheimer mejor que algunos escáneres cerebrales y pruebas genéticas. Ofrece a los médicos una forma sencilla de detectar a personas que probablemente desarrollarán problemas de memoria años antes de los síntomas. Esto podría ayudar a seleccionar quiénes pueden participar en estudios de prevención o recibir tratamiento temprano cuando haya nuevos medicamentos.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren confirmar estos resultados en grupos más grandes y diversos y durante más tiempo. También están probando nuevos tratamientos para frenar o detener Alzheimer antes de que aparezcan los síntomas. Si tienen éxito, este análisis podría convertirse en una herramienta común para guiar el cuidado temprano, similar a cómo el colesterol ayuda a prevenir enfermedades del corazón.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un simple análisis de sangre que mide p-tau217 puede identificar a personas con mayor riesgo de Alzheimer años antes de los síntomas, abriendo la puerta a la prevención y tratamiento temprano.
